The salt had a way of getting into everything. It settled in the creases of Elias’s knuckles, crusted in the corners of his eyes, and seemed to weigh down his very soul. For thirty years, he had tended the Gull’s Beak Lighthouse, a jagged tooth of granite jutting out into the North Atlantic. His life was measured in rotations of the great Fresnel lens and the rhythmic crash of waves against the rocks below.

It was a Tuesday in late November, the kind of day where the sky and the sea merged into a single, bruised purple. The storm had passed, leaving behind a debris field of kelp, driftwood, and the occasional plastic bottle. Elias was walking the shoreline, his boots squelching in the wet sand, when a glint of green caught his eye.

It wasn’t plastic. It was glass, thick and old, half-buried in a tangle of seaweed.

He dug it out with his gloved hands. The bottle was dark emerald, sealed with wax that had hardened into a black, waxy lump. Inside, rolled tightly, was a scrap of parchment.
